Grandma's pierogi recipe — finally got her to dictate it properly instead of the usual 'add flour until it feels right.'

Dough: 500g all-purpose flour, 1 large egg, 200ml warm water, pinch of salt, 2 tablespoons sour cream. Mix flour and salt, make a well, add egg and sour cream, then gradually add warm water while kneading. Knead for 8-10 minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough should be soft but not sticky — if it sticks to your hands, add flour a tablespoon at a time. Cover with a damp cloth and let rest 30 minutes minimum. She says an hour is better.

Filling (potato and cheese — the classic): Boil 1kg of potatoes until very soft, drain completely. Mash while hot — no lumps allowed. She's very strict about this. Add 300g of twarog (farmer's cheese), one large diced onion fried in butter until golden, salt and white pepper to taste. Mix everything while potatoes are still warm so the cheese melts slightly. Let cool before filling.

Assembly: Roll dough thin — about 2mm. Cut circles with a glass (she uses a specific glass that's about 8cm diameter). Place a tablespoon of filling on each circle, fold in half, press edges firmly with a fork. She says the secret is not overfilling — leave a good margin or they'll burst when boiling.

Boil in salted water for 3-4 minutes after they float. Serve with fried onions, sour cream, and optionally crispy bacon bits. Makes about 60 pierogi. They freeze beautifully — lay flat on a tray, freeze, then transfer to bags.

Book notes: 'Thinking in Systems' by Donella Meadows. Finished reading today.

Core thesis: Most of the world's problems — economic, environmental, social — arise from our failure to understand the systems we operate in. We focus on individual events and actors rather than the structures and feedback loops that produce those events.

Key concepts:

Stocks and Flows: A stock is any quantity that accumulates or depletes over time (water in a bathtub, money in a bank account, carbon in the atmosphere). Flows are the rates of change — inflows add to stocks, outflows deplete them. The critical insight is that stocks change slowly even when flows change quickly. This is why systems have momentum and why policies often take much longer to show effects than politicians promise.

Feedback Loops: Balancing loops push a system toward equilibrium (thermostat, population with limited food). Reinforcing loops amplify change in one direction (compound interest, viral spread, erosion of trust). Systems with dominant reinforcing loops are inherently unstable — they grow exponentially until they hit a constraint.

Delays: The time gap between an action and its visible effect. Delays are the most common source of oscillation in systems. Classic example: the shower temperature problem. You turn the hot tap, nothing happens for 30 seconds, so you turn it more, then suddenly it's scalding. In business, this manifests as overinvestment during booms and overcuts during downturns.

Leverage Points: Places where small interventions can produce large changes. Meadows ranks them from least to most effective: parameters (subsidies, taxes), buffer sizes, stock-and-flow structures, delays, feedback loops, information flows, system rules, self-organization, system goals, and paradigm shifts. The most common interventions (adjusting numbers) are the least effective. The most powerful (changing paradigms) are the hardest.

Bounded Rationality: Every actor in a system makes decisions based on incomplete information and limited cognitive capacity. No one is 'irrational' — they're rational within their own context and constraints. The problem is that individual rational decisions can produce collectively irrational outcomes (tragedy of the commons, arms races, traffic jams).

Practical takeaways for my work:
- When diagnosing problems, always ask 'what feedback loop is driving this behavior?' before asking 'who is responsible?'
- Be suspicious of policies that promise quick results in systems with long delays.
- Pay attention to information flows. Often the most effective intervention is simply making hidden information visible (carbon emissions labels, real-time energy dashboards, transparent pricing).
- Remember that the goal of the system defines its behavior more than any individual component. If a system isn't producing what you want, question the goal before tweaking parameters.

Rating: 9/10. Should be required reading for anyone in management, policy, or engineering. Re-read in 6 months.

Notes on distributed consensus algorithms — studying for the system design deep dive.

Paxos (Lamport, 1989/1998):
The OG consensus algorithm. Notoriously hard to understand (Lamport himself wrote the 'Paxos Made Simple' paper because nobody understood the first one). Three roles: Proposers, Acceptors, Learners. Two-phase protocol: Phase 1 (Prepare/Promise) — proposer picks a number n, sends Prepare(n) to acceptors. Acceptors promise not to accept anything with number less than n. If they already accepted something, they return it. Phase 2 (Accept/Accepted) — if proposer gets majority promises, it sends Accept(n, value) where value is either the highest-numbered previously accepted value or a new value if none were accepted. Acceptors accept if they haven't promised to something higher.

Key insight: Paxos guarantees safety (no two different values are chosen) but not liveness (the protocol can theoretically stall if proposers keep outbidding each other). In practice, a distinguished proposer (leader) is elected to avoid this.

Multi-Paxos: Single Paxos decides one value. Real systems need to decide a sequence of values (a replicated log). Multi-Paxos uses a stable leader who skips Phase 1 for subsequent instances, making it much more efficient. This is essentially what most production systems implement.

Raft (Ongaro & Ousterhout, 2014):
Designed explicitly for understandability. Same guarantees as Multi-Paxos but decomposed into independent subproblems: Leader Election, Log Replication, Safety.

Leader Election: Each server is in one of three states: Follower, Candidate, Leader. Time divided into terms (monotonically increasing integers). Each term has at most one leader. If a follower doesn't hear from a leader within a randomized timeout (150-300ms typically), it becomes a candidate, increments its term, votes for itself, and requests votes from others. Majority wins. The randomized timeout is crucial — it makes split votes unlikely.

Log Replication: The leader accepts client requests, appends them as entries in its log, then replicates them to followers via AppendEntries RPCs. An entry is committed once a majority of servers have written it. Committed entries are durable and will eventually be applied by all servers.

Safety: Raft adds an election restriction — a candidate must have all committed entries to win an election. This is enforced by including the candidate's last log entry in the vote request. Voters deny their vote if their log is more up-to-date.

Comparison:
- Raft is easier to implement correctly. Paxos implementations vary wildly because the paper leaves many practical details unspecified.
- Performance is roughly equivalent for normal operation. Both are leader-based and require majority agreement.
- Raft's term-based leader election is simpler than Paxos's proposal number scheme.
- Raft guarantees the leader has all committed entries; Paxos doesn't (the new leader might need to re-propose uncommitted entries).

Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT):
Both Paxos and Raft assume crash failures only — nodes either work correctly or stop. Byzantine failures mean nodes can behave arbitrarily (send conflicting messages, lie, collude). PBFT (Practical BFT by Castro & Liskov, 1999) tolerates up to f Byzantine failures with 3f+1 total nodes. Much more expensive — requires O(n^2) message complexity vs O(n) for crash-only consensus. Used in blockchain-adjacent systems but rarely in traditional distributed systems because the threat model doesn't justify the overhead.

Real-world implementations:
- etcd (Kubernetes): Raft
- ZooKeeper: ZAB (Zookeeper Atomic Broadcast, similar to Paxos)
- CockroachDB: Raft
- Google Spanner: Paxos
- MongoDB: Raft (since 3.2)

Next study topics: Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs), vector clocks, and the CALM theorem.

Japan trip planning notes — 2 weeks in April for cherry blossom season. Traveling with Kasia.

Flights:
Looked at several options. Best so far: LOT Polish Airlines Warsaw-Tokyo Narita, direct flight, departure March 29 arriving March 30 (11.5h). Return April 13 from Osaka Kansai to Warsaw via Helsinki (Finnair, 14h with layover). Open-jaw routing is key — fly into Tokyo, train down to Osaka, fly out from there. Saves backtracking. Current price for both: ~3200 PLN per person round trip. Need to book by end of this week as prices are climbing.

Itinerary draft:

Days 1-4: Tokyo
- Day 1 (March 30): Arrive Narita, take Narita Express to Shinjuku. Check into hotel. Jet lag recovery walk around Shinjuku Gyoen (one of the best cherry blossom spots apparently). Casual dinner at an izakaya.
- Day 2: Tsukiji Outer Market for breakfast. Sensoji Temple in Asakusa. Lunch in Asakusa. Afternoon: Akihabara for electronics and manga culture. Evening: Shibuya crossing, dinner in Shibuya.
- Day 3: Meiji Shrine in the morning (peaceful, forested). Harajuku and Takeshita Street. Lunch: Omotesando area. Afternoon: Teamlab Borderless (need to pre-book, tickets sell out weeks in advance — adding this to my todo). Evening: Roppongi for dinner.
- Day 4: Day trip to Kamakura — Great Buddha, Hasedera Temple, Komachi Street for shopping. Train from Shinjuku, about 1 hour. Or alternatively, Nikko — but Kasia prefers coast over mountains.

Days 5-7: Hakone + Mt. Fuji area
- Take the Romancecar from Shinjuku to Hakone. Stay at a traditional ryokan with onsen (hot spring bath). This is the splurge of the trip — budget 40,000-60,000 yen per night for a nice one. Kasia really wants the experience of sleeping on tatami and wearing yukata.
- Hakone loop tour: cable car, pirate ship on Lake Ashi, Owakudani volcanic valley. If weather cooperates, views of Mt. Fuji from here.
- Optional: Fuji Five Lakes area if we want more Fuji time, but might be overkill with Hakone.

Days 8-10: Kyoto
- Shinkansen from Hakone/Odawara to Kyoto (about 2.5 hours). This is where the JR Pass pays for itself.
- Day 8: Eastern Kyoto — Fushimi Inari (go early, 6am, to avoid crowds), Kiyomizudera, walk through Higashiyama district, Gion in the evening.
- Day 9: Northern Kyoto — Kinkakuji (Golden Pavilion), Ryoanji (rock garden), Arashiyama bamboo grove, Monkey Park. Rent bikes for this day — Kyoto is very flat and bike-friendly.
- Day 10: Nara day trip (45 min from Kyoto). Todaiji Temple with the massive bronze Buddha. Feed the deer in Nara Park. This is supposed to be very fun. Back to Kyoto for evening: Pontocho alley for dinner.

Days 11-12: Osaka
- Train to Osaka (15 min from Kyoto). Osaka is the food capital.
- Dotonbori area: street food crawl. Must try: takoyaki (octopus balls), okonomiyaki (savory pancake), kushikatsu (deep fried skewers), gyoza.
- Osaka Castle and its park — also great for cherry blossoms.
- Shinsekai area for retro vibes and more kushikatsu.
- Kasia wants to visit a cat cafe and do a cooking class for ramen. Need to research options.

Days 13-14: Buffer / extras
- Keep flexible for weather, fatigue, or discoveries along the way.
- Possible additions: Himeji Castle (1h from Osaka, Japan's most spectacular castle), or a sake brewery tour in Fushimi.

Budget estimates (per person, PLN):
- Flights: 3,200
- JR Pass (14 days): 1,800
- Accommodation: 7,000 (mix of mid-range hotels and one ryokan splurge)
- Food: 3,500 (eating well but not fine dining every night)
- Activities/entrance fees: 1,000
- Shopping/souvenirs: 1,500
- Transport (non-JR): 500
- Buffer: 1,500
Total estimate: ~20,000 PLN per person

To-do before booking:
1. Book flights this week
2. Order JR Pass online (cheaper than buying in Japan)
3. Book TeamLab tickets
4. Reserve ryokan in Hakone (popular ones sell out months ahead for cherry blossom)
5. Check if we need to activate any travel insurance
6. Download offline maps and translation app
7. Get pocket WiFi rental arranged for pickup at Narita

Monthly health and fitness review — February 2026.

Weight: Started the month at 84.2kg, ending at 82.8kg. That's 1.4kg down, which is right in the 0.5-0.75% per week range I'm targeting. The slow approach is working and I'm not feeling deprived.

Nutrition: Averaged about 2,100 calories per day according to MyFitnessPal. Protein intake was solid — hitting 140-160g most days through a combination of chicken, eggs, Greek yogurt, and one protein shake on training days. Biggest struggle remains weekends. Saturday dinners out tend to blow the calorie budget, but I've stopped stressing about individual days and focusing on weekly averages instead.

Meal prep has been a game changer. Spending 2 hours on Sunday cooking chicken thighs, rice, and roasted vegetables gives me lunch for the entire workweek. Cost is way down too — probably spending 30% less on food than when I was buying lunch daily.

Training: Got in 14 sessions this month out of a planned 16. Missed two due to that cold I had in the second week. Running a Push/Pull/Legs split, hitting everything twice per week.

Strength progress:
- Bench press: 80kg x 6 up from 77.5kg x 6. Slow but steady.
- Squat: 100kg x 8 up from 95kg x 8. Squats are finally feeling natural. That cue about 'spreading the floor with your feet' really clicked.
- Deadlift: 130kg x 5. Haven't pushed this up yet because I want form to be rock solid before adding weight. Got a form check from Marek and he said hip hinge looks good but I'm rounding my upper back slightly at the top. Going to focus on keeping chest proud through lockout.
- Overhead press: Still stuck at 50kg x 5. This lift just doesn't want to move. Going to try micro-loading with 0.5kg plates.

Cardio: Added two 30-minute zone 2 sessions per week (heart rate 130-145 bpm). Using the rowing machine because it's easier on my knees than running. Resting heart rate has dropped from 68 to 63 over the past two months, which is a good sign of cardiovascular adaptation.

Sleep: This is the weak link. Averaging 6.5 hours according to my watch. Need to get this to 7.5-8 hours. The main issue is screen time before bed. Going to try a hard cutoff at 10pm — phone goes in the kitchen, read a physical book until sleepy. Magnesium glycinate before bed has helped with sleep quality even if duration isn't great yet.

Goals for March:
- Hit all 16 training sessions
- Break through the 50kg OHP plateau
- Average 7+ hours of sleep
- Continue the slow cut — target 81.5kg by month end
- Book a sports massage. Haven't had one in months and my right trap is perpetually tight.

Brainstorm notes for the SaaS product idea — internal tool for engineering team productivity analytics. Working title: DevPulse.

Problem statement:
Engineering managers have poor visibility into team health and productivity. They rely on gut feeling, occasional 1-on-1s, and crude metrics like story points or lines of code. These metrics are either gameable, misleading, or both. Meanwhile, teams are burning out, context switching constantly, and spending huge amounts of time in meetings and on toil work — but nobody has data to quantify this.

Existing solutions and why they fall short:
- Jira/Linear dashboards: Show throughput (issues completed) but not effort or quality. A team can close lots of small tickets while the important work stalls.
- GitHub analytics (Copilot metrics, etc.): Too code-centric. Engineering work involves architecture, code review, mentoring, incident response, documentation. Measuring only commits misses half the job.
- Pluralsight Flow / Jellyfish: Enterprise-grade, expensive (we're talking $30-50 per developer per month), and overly complex. They try to measure 'developer experience' with surveys and integrations but the setup cost is enormous.
- Swarmia / DX: Closer to what I'm imagining but still heavy on the 'measure everything' approach. I think there's room for something more opinionated and lightweight.

Our angle — the hypothesis:
Engineering productivity is primarily destroyed by three things: excessive context switching, meeting overload, and unclear priorities. If you can measure and visualize just these three, you give managers 80% of the insight they need to improve team effectiveness.

Proposed features (MVP):

1. Context Switch Index:
Integrate with calendar and code tools (GitHub/GitLab). Map the developer's day into blocks: coding, reviewing, meetings, Slack. Calculate a 'fragmentation score' — how many times per day does a developer switch between deep work and shallow work? Research (Newport, Mark) shows that every context switch costs 15-25 minutes of recovery. A developer with 8 context switches per day is losing 2-3 hours to transitions. Visualize this per person and per team, with trends over time.

2. Meeting Load Dashboard:
Pull calendar data. Show: total meeting hours per week per person, percentage of week in meetings, meeting-free blocks available for deep work, recurring vs ad-hoc meeting ratio. Flag individuals who are above threshold (e.g., >15 hours/week in meetings). Research from Microsoft shows developers who have 2+ hour uninterrupted blocks are 30% more productive. Show how many of these blocks each person has.

3. Priority Clarity Score:
Integrate with project management tool (Linear, Jira). For each developer, calculate: how many active items do they have? How often do priorities change (items reprioritized or reassigned mid-sprint)? What's the ratio of planned vs unplanned work? Teams with high priority churn are typically struggling with unclear product direction or firefighting culture.

4. Weekly Digest:
Automatic email/Slack summary sent to managers on Monday morning: here's how last week looked for your team. Highlight concerning patterns (someone had 20 hours of meetings, another person had zero code review time, a third person's priorities changed 4 times). Make it actionable: 'Consider canceling the Wednesday sync for Alex — they have no deep work blocks on Wednesdays.'

Technical architecture thoughts:
- Data sources: Google Calendar API, GitHub/GitLab webhooks, Slack API, Linear/Jira API
- Backend: Node.js or Python. Probably Python for data processing. Could use TypeScript since that's what I know best.
- Database: PostgreSQL for relational data, maybe ClickHouse or TimescaleDB for time series analytics at scale
- Frontend: React dashboard, keep it simple. Recharts or similar for visualization.
- Auth: OAuth with Google Workspace / GitHub SSO. Target audience already has these.
- Deployment: Start with a simple VPS (Railway or Fly.io). Don't overengineer infrastructure before product-market fit.

Business model:
- Free tier: up to 5 developers, basic metrics, 30-day history
- Team plan: $12/developer/month, full analytics, 12-month history, Slack integration
- Enterprise: Custom pricing, SSO, on-premise option, dedicated support

Target customer: Series A-C startups with 20-100 engineers. Big enough to have management overhead, small enough that they can't afford (or don't want) enterprise solutions.

Go-to-market:
- Build in public on Twitter/X and LinkedIn. Engineering leadership content performs well.
- Launch on Product Hunt
- Create a free 'Developer Time Audit' tool that analyzes a team's calendar data and produces a report. Use this as a lead magnet.
- Partner with engineering coaching/consulting firms for referrals

Risks and concerns:
- Privacy: Developers are extremely sensitive about being monitored. The product must be positioned as a tool FOR developers and managers to improve work quality, not a surveillance tool. Transparent about data collection, let individuals see their own data, never expose individual metrics to upper management without consent.
- Data accuracy: Calendar data is notoriously messy (tentative events, all-day events that aren't real meetings, etc.). Need good heuristics for cleaning data.
- Adoption: Getting developers to connect their accounts requires trust. SOC 2 compliance will probably be necessary even for the early stage.

Next steps:
1. Talk to 10 engineering managers about their pain points. Validate the hypothesis.
2. Build a scrappy prototype that just does the meeting load analysis (simplest data source, highest pain).
3. Test it internally with our own team data.
4. Iterate based on feedback before touching the other features.

Detailed notes from the StaffPlus London conference, February 2026. Capturing the key talks and insights while they're fresh.

Keynote: 'The Staff Engineer's Role in Organizational Design' by Charity Majors

Charity argued that staff engineers have more influence over organizational design than they realize — and that this influence is actually their most important lever. The core idea: technical architecture and org structure are mirrors of each other (Conway's Law), but most staff engineers only try to change the technical architecture and ignore the organizational side.

Examples she gave:
- If your services have unclear ownership boundaries, it's not a technical problem — it's an org problem. The fix isn't better documentation, it's clearer team charters.
- If deployments are slow because they require coordination between teams, the technical solution (monorepo, better CI) is less effective than the org solution (give teams full ownership of their deployment pipeline).
- If code review queues are long, it's not because people are lazy — it's because the incentive structure rewards shipping your own code more than reviewing others'. The staff engineer's job is to make the org see code review as a first-class activity.

Actionable framework she proposed: Before writing any technical design document, write a 'Human Systems Design' document that answers: Who needs to coordinate? What are the incentive structures? Where are the communication bottlenecks? What skills need to exist in the team for this to succeed? If the human system isn't set up correctly, the technical system will fail regardless of how good the architecture is.

Talk 2: 'Debugging Production Incidents as a Leadership Skill' by Laura Nolan (ex-Google SRE)

Laura's premise: how you handle incidents reveals and shapes engineering culture more than any handbook or values document. The staff engineer sets the tone.

Key patterns she's observed in great incident responders:

1. Narrate everything out loud (or in the incident channel). 'I'm looking at the error rate dashboard. I see a spike starting at 14:32. Correlating with recent deploys...' This isn't just for documentation — it slows down your thinking, prevents tunnel vision, and brings others along so they can catch things you miss.

2. Timebox hypothesis testing. 'I think it might be the database. I'm going to spend 5 minutes checking connection pools and query latency. If that doesn't show anything, I'll move to the network layer.' Without timeboxes, people go down rabbit holes for 45 minutes while the incident burns.

3. Separate the fix from the investigation. The goal during an incident is to restore service, not to understand root cause. These are different activities that require different approaches. Roll back first, investigate later. She's seen incidents last 3x longer than necessary because the on-call person was trying to understand why instead of just reverting the last deploy.

4. Name the unknown unknowns. Explicitly say 'Here's what we don't know yet: we don't know if this is affecting all users or just a subset. We don't know if this started before or after the deploy. We don't know if the European region is also affected.' This prevents the team from assuming things that haven't been verified.

Post-incident reviews: Laura strongly advocates for 'learning reviews' not 'post-mortems.' The word matters because it frames the activity as learning, not blame. The review should produce insights, not action items. Her template: What happened? What surprised us? What did we learn about how our system behaves? What mental models were wrong? She explicitly bans 'so-and-so should have done X' language.

Talk 3: 'Writing Technical Strategy Documents That Actually Get Read' by Will Larson

Will's observation: most strategy documents fail not because the strategy is wrong, but because the document is unreadable. Engineering leaders write 20-page documents full of abstract principles and wonder why nobody follows them.

His formula for effective strategy documents:

1. Diagnosis (1-2 pages max): What's the problem we're solving? Be specific and evidence-based. 'Our deployment pipeline takes 45 minutes, which means engineers deploy at most twice per day, which means bug fixes take 24+ hours to reach production.' Not: 'Our deployment process needs improvement.'

2. Guiding policies (1 page): The principles that will guide decisions. These should be opinionated and constraining. 'We will optimize for deployment speed over deployment safety, accepting some increase in rollback frequency.' A policy that doesn't rule out options isn't a policy — it's a wish.

3. Coherent actions (1-2 pages): The specific things we're going to do. Each action should clearly follow from the diagnosis and policies. 'We will move to trunk-based development. We will replace our integration test suite with contract tests. We will implement automatic rollback on error rate spike.'

4. What we're NOT doing (half page): This is the most important section. Every strategy implies things that you're choosing not to do. Make them explicit. 'We are NOT investing in preview environments. We are NOT migrating to a monorepo. We are NOT building a custom deployment platform.' This prevents scope creep and manages expectations.

Total document: 5 pages max. Will says if it's longer than that, you don't understand the strategy well enough to explain it. Cut until it hurts, then cut some more.

His other key point: strategy documents should be updated, not replaced. Version them. When the strategy evolves, edit the existing document and note what changed and why. This builds institutional memory. A series of disconnected strategy documents is an organizational antipattern.

Talk 4: 'The Economics of Technical Decisions' by Kellan Elliott-McCrea (former CTO Etsy)

Kellan's talk was about bringing economic thinking to technical decisions. Core argument: engineers make economic tradeoffs constantly but rarely use economic language, which means decisions are made based on vibes rather than analysis.

Framework he proposed:

Every technical decision has four costs:
1. Build cost: How much effort to implement?
2. Maintenance cost: What's the ongoing operational burden?
3. Opportunity cost: What else could we be doing instead?
4. Coordination cost: How much cross-team work is needed?

Engineers chronically underestimate maintenance and coordination costs while overestimating build costs. The 'build vs buy' decision is almost always wrong because people compare build cost to buy cost without accounting for maintenance cost (for built solutions) and coordination cost (for integrating bought solutions).

His rule of thumb: if a built solution will be maintained by fewer than 2 full-time engineers, you probably shouldn't build it. Anything maintained 'on the side' will eventually rot. If you can't dedicate a team to it, buy it or use a managed service.

Relevant example: The 'let's build our own deployment pipeline' decision. Build cost seems reasonable — maybe 3 engineer-months. But maintenance cost over 3 years? Probably 1.5 FTE equivalent, plus incident response, plus the opportunity cost of those engineers not working on product features. Meanwhile, a managed solution (Vercel, Railway, etc.) costs $X/month but has zero maintenance cost. The math almost always favors buying, but the 'build instinct' is strong because engineers enjoy building things.

Overall conference reflection:
The consistent theme across all talks: the staff engineer's job is fundamentally about systems thinking — not just technical systems, but human systems. Technical skills are table stakes. The differentiator is the ability to see the full picture: technology, people, incentives, economics, and how they all interact.

Books mentioned across talks that I should read:

- 'Thinking in Systems' by Donella Meadows (already read this! see my earlier notes)
- 'The Manager's Path' by Camille Fournier
- 'Team Topologies' by Skelton & Pais
- 'Accelerate' by Forsgren, Humble & Kim

Deep dive notes on WebAssembly (Wasm) — current state, use cases, and where it's heading. Compiled from multiple sources and my own experiments this week.

Background and motivation:
WebAssembly is a binary instruction format for a stack-based virtual machine. Designed as a compilation target for languages like C, C++, Rust, Go, etc. Originally created to run near-native performance code in web browsers, but it's rapidly expanding beyond the browser. The key properties that make it interesting: sandboxed execution (secure by default), near-native performance, language-agnostic, and portable across platforms.

The origin story matters for understanding design decisions: Wasm grew out of asm.js, Mozilla's experiment with a strict subset of JavaScript that could be AOT-compiled. Google was working on NaCl (Native Client) for Chrome. Both approaches had limitations — asm.js was still limited by JavaScript's semantics, and NaCl was Chrome-only and architecturally complex. Wasm was the industry compromise: a proper bytecode format that all browser vendors agreed on. The MVP shipped in all major browsers in 2017.

Current state (2026):

Browser Wasm is mature and widely used. Major applications:
- Figma: Their entire rendering engine is C++ compiled to Wasm. This is probably the most cited success story. The performance is indistinguishable from native.
- Google Earth: Uses Wasm for the 3D rendering pipeline in the web version.
- AutoCAD: Brought their desktop CAD application to the web via Wasm. Decades of C++ code running in the browser.
- Photoshop Web: Adobe's web version of Photoshop uses Wasm for performance-critical image processing.
- Game engines: Unity and Unreal both support Wasm as a build target. Most browser-based games with 3D graphics are using it.
- Audio/Video: FFmpeg compiled to Wasm allows video processing entirely client-side. Privacy-preserving because media never leaves the browser.

Recent spec additions that matter:
- SIMD (shipped): Single Instruction, Multiple Data operations for parallel numeric processing. Critical for codecs, image processing, ML inference.
- Threads (shipped): SharedArrayBuffer-based threading. Enables true parallelism, not just concurrency. Game-changer for applications like video encoding.
- Exception handling (shipped): Proper try/catch semantics instead of the previous hack using JavaScript exceptions. Makes C++ exception handling work correctly and efficiently.
- GC (Garbage Collection) proposal (shipping): This is the big one for 2025-2026. Allows Wasm modules to create and manage GC-managed objects directly, without going through JavaScript. This makes languages like Kotlin, Dart, Java, and C# much more efficient as Wasm compilation targets because they don't need to ship their own GC implementation.
- Component Model (in progress): The most ambitious proposal. Defines how Wasm modules can compose together with well-defined interfaces. Think of it as a universal ABI for Wasm components. This is what makes the 'Wasm outside the browser' story really compelling.

Wasm outside the browser — this is where the excitement is:

WASI (WebAssembly System Interface):
WASI provides a standardized set of APIs for Wasm modules to interact with the operating system: filesystem, networking, clocks, random numbers, etc. Think of it as the POSIX of WebAssembly. The key insight is that WASI uses a capability-based security model — a Wasm module can only access resources it's been explicitly granted. You can run untrusted code and give it access to exactly one directory and nothing else. No ambient authority.

WASI Preview 2 (the current stable version) uses the Component Model's WIT (WebAssembly Interface Type) format for defining interfaces. This means WASI is essentially a collection of WIT interfaces that any Wasm runtime can implement.

Server-side Wasm runtimes:
- Wasmtime (Bytecode Alliance / Mozilla): The reference implementation. Most mature, best standards compliance. Written in Rust.
- Wasmer: Focuses on ease of use and packaging. Has a package registry (wapm.io) for distributing Wasm modules. Supports running Wasm from many host languages.
- WasmEdge (CNCF project): Optimized for cloud-native and edge computing. Used in container ecosystems.
- V8: Google's JavaScript engine also runs Wasm, so Node.js can execute Wasm modules natively.

Cloud and edge computing:

This is where Solomon Hykes' famous quote comes in: 'If WASM+WASI existed in 2008, we wouldn't have needed to create Docker.' The idea is that Wasm provides what containers provide (isolation, portability) but with much lower overhead:
- Wasm modules start in microseconds vs milliseconds for containers
- Wasm modules are typically 1-10MB vs 100MB-1GB for container images
- Wasm's sandbox is formally verifiable; container isolation relies on Linux kernel features that have a larger attack surface
- Wasm is truly cross-platform — the same module runs on ARM and x86 without separate builds

Fermyon Spin: Framework for building serverless Wasm applications. Defines a simple model: your app handles HTTP requests, each handler is a Wasm component. Cold start times are under 1ms. They have a cloud platform (Fermyon Cloud) and an open-source runtime.

Cosmonic: Takes the actor model approach — each Wasm component is an actor that communicates via well-defined interfaces. Built on wasmCloud. Interesting for distributed systems because you can deploy actors across multiple nodes and the runtime handles networking.

Fastly Compute@Edge: One of the first commercial Wasm-at-the-edge platforms. Your CDN logic runs as Wasm modules at Fastly's edge nodes. Custom request routing, authentication, A/B testing — all at the edge in Wasm.

Cloudflare Workers: Originally V8 isolates (JavaScript), now also supports Wasm modules. The performance characteristics are impressive — you get sub-millisecond cold starts and your code runs in 300+ data centers worldwide.

Plugin systems:
This might be the most practical near-term use case for Wasm outside browsers. Instead of implementing a scripting language or an RPC-based plugin system, you let users write plugins in any language, compile to Wasm, and run them in your application's sandbox.

Examples:
- Envoy Proxy: Uses Wasm for custom filters. Network operators can extend proxy behavior without recompiling Envoy.
- Zed Editor: Uses Wasm for language server extensions and themes.
- Shopify Functions: Merchants write custom logic (discounts, shipping rules) as Wasm modules. Runs in Shopify's infrastructure with strict sandboxing and resource limits.
- Extism: A framework specifically for building Wasm plugin systems. Provides SDKs for host applications (in Rust, Go, Python, Ruby, etc.) and PDKs for plugin authors. We should evaluate this for IntexuraOS — could be a way to let users extend the system with custom action types.

Blockchain and smart contracts:
Ethereum's EVM is being complemented by Wasm-based execution environments. Polkadot uses Wasm natively for its runtime. The appeal: Wasm is more efficient than EVM bytecode, supports more source languages, and has better tooling. Near Protocol, Cosmos/CosmWasm, and others are all-in on Wasm for smart contracts.

Machine Learning inference:
Wasm + SIMD enables running ML models directly in the browser or at the edge without sending data to a server. ONNX Runtime has a Wasm backend. TensorFlow Lite supports Wasm. For privacy-sensitive applications (medical imaging, on-device NLP), this is significant — the data never leaves the user's device.

Limitations and challenges:

1. Performance ceiling: Wasm is 'near-native' but not native. Benchmarks typically show 1.1x-2x overhead compared to native code, depending on the workload. For compute-heavy, tight-loop code, this gap is shrinking. For code with lots of indirect calls or memory access patterns that don't play well with Wasm's linear memory, the gap can be larger.

2. Debugging: Still painful. Source maps for Wasm exist but aren't as mature as JavaScript source maps. Debugging a C++ application compiled to Wasm in Chrome DevTools works but is clunky. The toolchain is improving but it's a real barrier for adoption.

3. DOM access: Wasm can't directly manipulate the browser DOM. All DOM interactions go through JavaScript interop. This is by design (the DOM is a specific browser API, not a general computing primitive) but it means Wasm doesn't replace JavaScript for typical web development. It complements it for performance-critical computations.

4. Ecosystem maturity: While the core spec is stable, many proposals are still in flux. WASI is still evolving. The Component Model is powerful but complex. Library support varies by language — Rust has excellent Wasm support, Python's is improving (via Pyodide), Java/Kotlin are getting there with the GC proposal.

5. Binary size: Wasm modules compiled from languages with large standard libraries (Go, Java) can be quite large. A simple 'Hello World' in Go compiled to Wasm is ~2MB. Rust and C++ are much leaner. TinyGo helps for Go but doesn't support the full standard library.

My predictions for the next 2-3 years:
- The Component Model will ship and become the standard way to compose Wasm modules. This unlocks the 'universal plugin system' vision.
- At least one major cloud provider will offer a Wasm-native serverless platform that directly competes with Lambda/Cloud Functions on cold start time and cost.
- AI inference at the edge via Wasm will become mainstream. Every CDN provider will offer it.
- The browser use case will plateau — most apps that benefit from Wasm in the browser are already using it. The growth will be server-side and edge.
- Wasm will become a standard component in CI/CD pipelines — running linting, testing, and build tools as Wasm modules for reproducibility and portability.

Relevance to IntexuraOS:
- Consider using Wasm for the plugin/extension system. Users could write custom action processors in any language.
- The Extism framework looks promising for this — evaluate it.
- Edge computing angle: could we run the command classifier at the edge using Wasm? Would reduce latency and potentially cost.
- Research whether Wasm-based function execution could replace some of our Cloud Functions workloads.
